details.heading: How the coupling works
details.text: The trailer kingpin enters the throat of the fifth wheel and is captured by its locking mechanism. The plate carries trailer weight and permits the tractor and trailer to pivot. details.heading: What to look for

details.heading: Typical path and its limits
details.text: A common modern arrangement puts a diesel oxidation catalyst and particulate filter upstream of DEF dosing and an SCR catalyst; some systems combine or rearrange functions. Trace the specific engine’s service diagram instead of identifying order solely by exterior housings.

details.heading: Different jobs
details.text: The oxidation catalyst promotes oxidation of certain exhaust pollutants, the DPF traps particulate matter, and SCR uses a reductant derived from DEF to reduce nitrogen oxides. Sensors and controls monitor the system.

details.heading: Separate fluids and paths
details.text: Diesel fuel supplies the engine. DEF is a urea-and-water solution used by an SCR system and is metered into exhaust downstream of the engine. Their tanks, fillers, and plumbing are separate; verify the labels before filling.

details.heading: Contamination matters
details.text: Fuel in a DEF tank or DEF in a fuel tank can damage equipment. Stop filling and follow the manufacturer’s response procedure if the wrong fluid is added.

details.heading: Who does what

details.heading: Check the transaction
details.text: Identify contracting parties, operating authority, cargo responsibility, payment terms, and who communicates changes. A broker’s arrangement does not by itself mean the broker physically operates the truck.

title: Warning Devices After a Highway Stop (U.S.)
summary: A real reflective warning triangle illustrates one device; U.S. commercial-vehicle rules govern the number, timing, and placement.

items.label: REFLECTIVE EMERGENCY WARNING TRIANGLE
items.alt: Red reflective warning triangle standing beside a roadside.
items.caption: A real portable warning triangle photographed beside a road. The source photograph is from Finland and illustrates the device itself, not the U.S. placement pattern.

items.label: WHEEL CHOCK PHOTO
items.alt: Photograph of a wheel chock placed against a trailer wheel.
items.caption: A wheel chock is separate from the roadside warning devices required after a highway stop.

facts.what: For a U.S. commercial motor vehicle stopped on the traveled portion or shoulder for a reason other than a necessary traffic stop, federal rules require hazard flashers and external warning devices.
facts.does: The current rule generally requires the driver to place the required devices as soon as possible and within 10 minutes, at prescribed positions around the vehicle.
facts.where: Three warning devices are required; placement depends on roadway type, direction of traffic, and visibility. Check 49 CFR § 392.22 and § 393.95.

note: This photograph shows one triangle only and is not a placement diagram. Exceptions apply; follow the current regulation, safe positioning practices, and carrier procedures. The gallery intentionally uses no map or infographic.

sources.title: 49 CFR § 392.22 — Emergency signals; stopped commercial motor vehicles
49 CFR § 393.95 — Emergency equipment on all power units

details.heading: Placement depends on the road
details.text: For common two-way roads, federal rules generally call for one device near the traffic side of the vehicle and devices 100 feet in each direction. On a divided or one-way road, the typical pattern is behind the vehicle at 10, 100, and 200 feet. Curves, hills, hazardous materials, and other conditions can change requirements; consult the current rule.

title: CVSA Level I vs. II vs. III

items.label: TRUCK AT OREGON PORT OF ENTRY
items.alt: An inspector in reflective clothing examines the underside of a Freightliner semitrailer at an inspection pit.

items.label: ODOT COMMERCIAL TRUCK SAFETY ENFORCEMENT
items.alt: Oregon Department of Transportation photograph of a truck receiving a warning during an enforcement campaign.
items.caption: The source identifies an enforcement campaign, not a CVSA inspection level.
items.credit: Oregon Department of Transportation · CC BY 2.0

items.label: REFLECTIVE WARNING TRIANGLE
items.alt: Photograph of a red reflective roadside warning triangle.
items.caption: A real reflective triangle is shown; this specific photo was taken in Finland and does not show U.S. placement distances.

facts.what: CVSA Level I covers driver credentials and records plus a detailed vehicle inspection; Level II is a driver-and-vehicle walk-around limited to items that can be checked without physically getting under the vehicle; Level III focuses on driver credentials and administrative items.
facts.does: The level describes the scope of an inspection, not a score or a guarantee that every jurisdiction conducts the same encounter.
facts.where: Use CVSA’s current North American Standard inspection guidance for the exact checklist and applicable exceptions.

note: The photograph is not evidence that a specific inspection level occurred. Level I, II, and III inspection scope is summarized from CVSA; details and procedures can change.

sources.title: Oregon DOT truck inspection photograph — Wikimedia Commons

details.heading: Level I
details.text: A comprehensive driver and vehicle inspection includes items requiring access under the vehicle as well as driver credentials and operating requirements.

details.heading: Level II
details.text: The walk-around driver and vehicle inspection covers items that can be examined without physically getting under the vehicle. It is not simply a shorter Level I with identical coverage.

details.heading: Level III
details.text: A driver, credential, and administrative inspection focuses on applicable driver-related requirements. Inspection results and out-of-service decisions depend on the actual findings and current criteria.

title: Truck Transmission Types
summary: Photographs show a truck gearbox cutaway and a Volvo I-Shift control unit; the controls and gearbox are different parts of a transmission system.

items.alt: Photograph of a cutaway truck gearbox at the DAF Museum.

items.alt: Photograph of an electronic pneumatic gear-change control unit identified as a truck semi-automatic unit.

facts.what: A truck transmission changes the relationship between engine speed and drive-wheel speed. Manual, automated manual (AMT), and automatic describe different shift/control strategies and hardware designs.
facts.does: The gearbox cutaway shows internal hardware while the I-Shift photograph shows a control component. They should not be treated as equivalent views of the same part.
facts.where: The gearbox sits behind the engine; driver controls are in the cab. Exact layout varies by truck.

details.heading: Manual, automated manual, automatic
details.text: A manual uses driver-controlled shifts and clutch operation. An automated manual automates clutch and gear selection in a geared transmission. A conventional automatic typically uses a torque converter and planetary gears; design and controls vary.

details.heading: Application matters
details.text: Gear selection depends on load, road speed, grade, engine torque, and the transmission’s shift strategy. A photographed selector alone does not identify internal hardware.

items.alt: Photograph of a universal joint in the driveshaft of an International cab-over tractor.

facts.what: The driveline carries torque from the transmission to the drive axle. A differential lets the left and right drive wheels turn at different speeds while receiving engine torque.
facts.does: A universal joint is a shaft connection; the differential is a gear assembly in the drive axle. They are separate components.
facts.where: Follow the path from transmission, along the driveshaft, to the drive-axle differential and axle shafts.

note: These photographs show specific hardware examples, not a complete modern U.S. tractor driveline. Service procedures depend on the vehicle and component manufacturer.

details.heading: Torque path
details.text: Torque flows from the transmission through driveshafts and joints to the drive axle. The final drive changes speed and torque; the differential allows wheels on the same axle to turn at different speeds in a turn.

details.heading: What an inspection can show
details.text: Leaks, damaged boots or guards, loose fittings, and visible joint damage are reasons for inspection. A photograph does not establish internal wear or a diagnosis.

title: Tire Count on a 5-Axle Tractor-Trailer

items.label: TRACTOR–TRAILER ORIENTATION
items.alt: Side view of a Volvo VNL 670 tractor with box trailer; axle count is not specified by the Commons source.

items.caption: This shows a tractor drive axle group; count the axle lines, not the number of tire sidewalls, when describing axles.

items.label: TRAILER REAR AXLE EXAMPLE
items.alt: Photograph of a historical heavy-transport semitrailer rear axle at a museum.
items.caption: This historic axle is not presented as a modern U.S. two-axle trailer configuration.

facts.what: For the common five-axle arrangement, the combination has 5 axle lines: 1 steer + 2 drive + 2 trailer. A conventional dual-tire setup commonly has 18 tires: 2 steer tires and 8 each on tractor drive and trailer axle groups.
facts.does: Axle count and tire count are not interchangeable. Lift axles, wide-base singles, different trailers, and special configurations change counts.
facts.where: Move front to back: tractor steer → tractor drive tandem → semitrailer tandem.

note: The Volvo side-view photo is not source-identified as five axles. The other photos show contextual axle groups and are not one combined rig. The 18-tire count is an illustrative common layout, not a universal rule.

sources.title: Context only — 49 CFR § 393.75: tire requirements, not axle or tire count

details.heading: Count the layout
details.text: A common configuration has one steering axle on the tractor, two tractor drive axles, and two trailer axles. With two steer tires and dual tires at both ends of each remaining axle, the arithmetic is 2 + 8 + 8 = 18 tires.

details.heading: Why the answer varies
details.text: Five axles describe axle lines, not a fixed number of tires. Wide-base single tires, lift axles, and other configurations can change the tire count; count the equipment actually present.

title: Minimum Tread Depth in the U.S.
summary: Close photographs show tire tread and damage; the U.S. federal minimum depends on tire position and is measured in major tread grooves.

items.label: TRUCK TIRE TREAD CLOSE-UP
items.alt: Close photograph of a truck tire mounted on a wheel.
items.caption: This racing-truck slick tire photo does not demonstrate a compliant commercial-road tread depth.

items.label: TREAD DAMAGE EXAMPLE
items.alt: Photograph of a truck tire with tread separation.
items.caption: Tread separation is prohibited independently of groove-depth measurement.

facts.what: Under 49 CFR § 393.75, steer tires on trucks and truck tractors require at least 4/32 inch in a major tread groove; other covered tires generally require at least 2/32 inch.
facts.does: The legal test is a groove-depth measurement at a major tread groove, excluding tie bars, humps, and fillets. Damage conditions can independently make a tire unsafe or noncompliant.
facts.where: Steer position has the 4/32-inch threshold; the general 2/32-inch threshold applies to other tires covered by the rule.

note: This is a U.S. federal baseline for covered commercial motor vehicles. State rules, special vehicles, tire specifications, and company policy can add requirements. The photos are not measuring tools.

details.heading: Federal measurement
details.text: For the front wheels of a bus, truck, or truck tractor, 49 CFR 393.75 specifies at least 4/32 inch when measured at any point on a major tread groove. Other covered tires require at least 2/32 inch when measured in a major tread groove. Measurements are not made where tie bars, humps, or fillets are located.

details.heading: Practical inspection
details.text: Use a tread-depth gauge in major grooves and inspect across the tread. Depth alone does not establish that a tire is safe: cuts, exposed cord, separation, and other defects have separate requirements. Additional state or operating requirements may apply.

title: Passive vs. Active vs. Parked Regen
summary: Photographs show real aftertreatment and engine hardware. Regeneration modes are operating states, so a still photograph cannot identify which mode is occurring.

items.label: HINO SCR / DPR ASSEMBLY
items.alt: Photograph of a Hino diesel exhaust treatment unit identified as SCR/DPR by its source.
items.caption: The photo documents aftertreatment hardware, not a visible active, passive, or parked regeneration event.

items.label: TRUCK TURBOCHARGER / EXHAUST BRAKE
items.alt: Close photograph of a truck-engine turbocharger and exhaust brake assembly.
items.caption: A turbocharger/exhaust-brake component view; no regeneration mode is visible.

items.label: TRUCK AIR COMPRESSOR
items.alt: Truck air compressor with Cummins branding visible on the housing.
items.caption: The image source identifies a truck air compressor; the Cummins name is visible on the photographed part. It is a photo of one component, not a complete engine layout.

facts.what: Passive regeneration uses exhaust heat already available to oxidize accumulated particulate matter; active strategies add heat or fuel when needed. Some vehicles request a stationary or parked regeneration.
facts.does: Passive, active, and parked describe different regeneration strategies or operating conditions. Exact indications, prerequisites, and instructions are vehicle-specific.
facts.where: Regeneration occurs in the diesel particulate filter (DPF) in the exhaust aftertreatment system.

note: EPA describes passive and active regeneration for diesel particulate filters. Follow the truck maker’s warnings and instructions; do not assume that every DPF has the same parked-regeneration procedure.

sources.title: EPA — Diesel Particulate Filter Operation and Maintenance

details.heading: Passive regeneration
details.text: Heat produced during normal operation can burn accumulated soot when exhaust conditions are sufficient. It may happen without the driver initiating an event.

details.heading: Active and parked regeneration
details.text: Active regeneration uses additional heat or fuel when needed; it can occur while driving or during a stationary event. A parked regeneration is a stationary procedure required by some systems under certain conditions. Follow the vehicle’s prompts and OEM instructions, including site and exhaust-clearance requirements.

details.heading: Soot and ash
details.text: Regeneration removes soot; noncombustible ash can still accumulate and eventually require filter service. Repeated requests or warning lights deserve diagnosis rather than repeated forced cycles.

title: Around What Temperature Does DEF Freeze?
summary: A real truck aftertreatment photograph provides context for DEF/SCR equipment. Freezing point is a fluid property, not visually detectable in a photograph.

items.label: SCR / DIESEL EXHAUST TREATMENT
items.alt: Photograph of a Hino diesel exhaust treatment unit identified as SCR/DPR by its source.

items.label: DIESEL TRACTOR CONTEXT
items.alt: Photograph of a Freightliner tractor parked at a California travel plaza.
items.caption: A diesel tractor context image; the source does not identify its emissions system or DEF tank position.

facts.what: DEF (diesel exhaust fluid) freezes at about 12°F (−11°C). Vehicle systems are designed to manage freezing and thawing, but details vary by model.
facts.does: Frozen DEF does not mean the fluid is permanently unusable. Do not add contaminants or heat it using an unapproved method; follow the vehicle operator manual.
facts.where: DEF is stored in a dedicated tank and metered into the exhaust aftertreatment system on SCR-equipped engines.

note: The two photographs are real vehicle/system context only; neither proves the pictured vehicle has the specific system described. The freeze point is approximate and product-specific guidance may apply.

sources.title: Cummins — 6 Answers About Diesel Exhaust Fluid

details.heading: Freeze and thaw
details.text: DEF freezes at about 12°F (−11°C). Vehicle systems designed for DEF generally include provisions for thawing; follow the equipment manual and protect DEF from contamination. Do not infer the fluid’s condition from the exterior of a truck.

facts.what: A common After Action Review (AAR) asks: What was supposed to happen? What actually happened? What went well and why? What can we improve or learn?
facts.does: An AAR is a structured, no-blame learning conversation after an event, exercise, shift, or project. Question wording varies by organization and context.
facts.where: Use the questions after an operation or incident, with people who participated and objective records where available.

note: AAR can mean other things in trucking and rail contexts. This entry uses the common After Action Review meaning; confirm that this is the intended expansion for your workplace.

sources.title: U.S. Fire Administration — After Action Review: A Valuable Learning Opportunity

details.heading: Turn observations into action
details.text: Compare the intended plan with a timeline and actual records, discuss what helped and what could improve, and assign specific follow-up actions. The wording and the meaning of AAR can differ by organization.

facts.what: A budget is an approved plan for a period. A forecast is a current estimate of expected results, updated as actual conditions change.
facts.does: Compare actual results and the latest forecast against the budget to identify timing, volume, rate, cost, and utilization differences. Accounting practices differ.
facts.where: A carrier may forecast freight volume, revenue, fuel, repairs, payroll, and equipment availability.

note: These photographs are operating context only; they do not show financial statements or establish any company’s performance.

sources.title: Context only — FMCSA — Motor carrier financial and operational context

details.heading: Different questions
details.text: A budget sets an approved target or spending authority for a period. A forecast estimates the likely outcome using information available now; a forecast can differ from the original budget.

details.heading: Example
details.text: A fleet budgets $10,000 for maintenance but forecasts $12,000 after an unexpected repair. Track the $2,000 variance and its causes rather than treating the forecast as automatic approval to spend.

title: DVIR Repair Loop

facts.what: A Driver Vehicle Inspection Report (DVIR) records reportable defects. The carrier repairs a defect likely to affect safe operation before dispatch and certifies correction or that correction was unnecessary, as required.
facts.does: The loop is report → evaluate → repair or determine no repair is needed → certify → retain records under applicable rules. A defect report is not itself proof that a repair was completed.
facts.where: The driver identifies vehicle condition; the carrier and maintenance process handle the required repair and certification steps.

note: The images are contextual photographs, not a sample DVIR form. Applicable exceptions and requirements should be checked against current FMCSA rules.

details.heading: Report and assess
details.text: A driver reports defects or deficiencies that could affect safe operation or cause a breakdown. Under the current federal rule, a no-defect report is not required when no defect or deficiency is discovered or reported; applicability, exceptions, state rules, and carrier policies still need checking.

details.heading: Repair and certify
details.text: Before dispatch, the carrier must correct reported defects likely to affect safe operation. The carrier or its agent certifies that the defect was corrected or that correction was unnecessary; the next driver reviews the last report and signs when required. Retain the report and certifications for the required period.

title: FMI 3–6 Usually Suggest…
summary: Photographs show real electrical/mechanical vehicle contexts, but an FMI code describes a diagnostic condition and cannot be read from the component photograph.

items.label: ENGINE-DRIVEN AIR COMPRESSOR

facts.what: In J1939 diagnostics, FMI 3 usually means voltage above normal or shorted high; FMI 4 means voltage below normal or shorted low; FMI 5 means current below normal or open circuit; FMI 6 means current above normal or grounded circuit.
facts.does: FMI wording is a general failure-mode description. The SPN, OEM diagnostic tree, circuit design, and test conditions are needed to diagnose the actual fault.
facts.where: Use the complete SPN/FMI and the specific OEM service information; do not replace a component based on FMI alone.

note: The word “usually” matters: codes and diagnostic tests are system-specific. The photos are real vehicle parts and do not show the electrical fault.

sources.title: Eaton ServiceRanger — Example OEM J1939 FMI definitions

details.heading: Interpret the code as a clue
details.text: FMI describes the type of abnormal condition associated with a suspect parameter; it does not identify the failed part. For example, a low-voltage indication may come from wiring, supply, sensor, or controller problems.

details.heading: Diagnostic sequence
details.text: Record the full SPN/FMI, occurrence count, operating conditions, and vehicle-specific fault information. Follow the OEM diagnostic procedure and electrical safety practices before replacing components.

details.text: The Caltrans comparison table identifies J560 circuit 4 as red for stop lamps and antilock devices. Caltrans uses a different wiring configuration, and other seven-way connector families and fleet modifications can differ.

details.heading: Verify before work
details.text: Confirm connector type, pin orientation, wiring diagram, and circuit function on the vehicle. Wire color alone is not proof of function, especially after repairs or modifications.

title: OEM vs. Aftermarket vs. Reman

items.caption: The source identifies the physical brake component, not its supply channel or refurbishment history.

facts.what: OEM parts are supplied by the original equipment manufacturer or its authorized channel; aftermarket parts are supplied by other manufacturers; remanufactured parts are used components restored to a defined process/specification.
facts.does: Part origin and remanufacturing status are determined from traceability, labeling, supplier documentation, and applicable warranty—not appearance alone.
facts.where: Compare part number, fitment, warranty, quality requirements, and supplier traceability for the specific application.

note: Neither photograph is verified as OEM, aftermarket, or remanufactured. These images show what kinds of components the terms can apply to, not a three-way product comparison.

sources.title: U.S. Federal Trade Commission — Buying auto parts and repair services

details.heading: Source versus condition
details.text: OEM and aftermarket describe supply or origin; remanufactured describes a restoration process. A part can be both OEM-supplied and remanufactured, so these labels are not mutually exclusive.

details.heading: Compare the actual part
details.text: Check fitment, specifications, warranty, core charges and return conditions, traceability, and the remanufacturer’s documented process. A used part is not automatically remanufactured.

title: Reorder Point Formula
summary: Real component photographs provide inventory examples; the reorder-point calculation is stated separately and does not appear in the images.

items.label: TRUCK AIR COMPRESSOR
items.alt: Photograph of a truck air compressor with Cummins branding.
items.caption: A real replacement-part category; this image does not show stock quantity or replenishment lead time.

items.label: SPRING-BRAKE CHAMBER
items.alt: Photograph of a truck spring-brake air cylinder.
items.caption: A real maintenance component, with no inventory level visible in the photo.

facts.what: A common reorder point is average demand during replenishment lead time plus safety stock: ROP = (average daily demand × lead-time days) + safety stock.
facts.does: The formula estimates when to trigger replenishment. Demand variability, supplier lead time, criticality, and review policy determine appropriate safety stock.
facts.where: Apply the calculation to a specific part number and unit of measure; do not mix eaches, kits, or service assemblies.

note: This is an inventory-planning formula, not a universal accounting rule. The photos show parts only; they do not depict on-hand quantities or supplier lead times.

sources.title: Context only — U.S. Small Business Administration — Manage inventory

details.heading: Worked example
details.text: If demand averages 4 filters per day, replenishment lead time is 5 days, and safety stock is 10 filters, reorder at 4 × 5 + 10 = 30 filters.

details.heading: What can invalidate it
details.text: Use consistent units and account for variability in demand and lead time. The formula triggers replenishment; order quantity is a separate decision, and open purchase orders affect inventory position.

title: Leading vs. Lagging Indicator
summary: Photographs show a roadside inspection and a documented tire-damage example. The images are operational context, not a carrier performance dashboard.

items.label: ROADSIDE INSPECTION CONTEXT
items.alt: Oregon Department of Transportation photograph of a truck at an inspection station.
items.caption: A real inspection setting that may relate to preventive safety activity; it is not itself a leading-indicator statistic.
items.credit: Oregon Department of Transportation · CC BY 2.0

items.label: TIRE FAILURE OUTCOME EXAMPLE
items.alt: Photograph of a truck tire with tread separation.
items.caption: A real tire damage example; it does not establish incident rate or root cause.

facts.what: A leading indicator tracks actions or conditions intended to prevent future outcomes, such as completed inspections or corrective actions. A lagging indicator tracks results after events, such as breakdowns or injuries.
facts.does: Indicators need clear definitions, denominators, time periods, and data quality. A single photograph is not a KPI.
facts.where: Use leading measures to monitor preventive work and lagging measures to monitor outcomes; review both together.

note: Examples vary by carrier and purpose. Avoid treating a count without context, exposure, or denominator as a meaningful rate.

details.heading: Use both kinds
details.text: Inspection completion or timely closure of defects can show whether a process is being performed. Breakdowns and injury counts describe outcomes that have already occurred.

details.heading: Avoid false confidence
details.text: A high completion rate is useful only if inspections are effective and defects are reported accurately. Pair activity measures with quality checks and outcome measures, and define the measurement period and denominator.

facts.what: A bill of lading (BOL) records shipment and carriage details and may serve as a receipt/contract document. A proof of delivery (POD) records delivery completion and may include receiver evidence.
facts.does: The BOL is associated with shipment pickup and carriage; POD evidence is associated with delivery. Electronic processes and contract requirements vary.
facts.where: Keep documents tied to the load/reference number and delivery event; follow shipper, broker, carrier, and customer requirements.

note: The photographs are contextual scenes, not legal forms or evidence of any particular shipment. Document requirements vary by mode and contract.

sources.title: 49 CFR § 373.101 — Bills of lading for for-hire, non-exempt carriers

details.heading: At pickup
details.text: The bill of lading identifies the shipment and parties and documents the goods tendered for carriage. Details, exceptions, signatures, and the applicable contract determine its legal effect.

details.heading: At delivery
details.text: Proof of delivery records evidence of delivery, often through a signed document or electronic record. Check delivery exceptions, dates, and customer requirements before billing; a BOL and POD may be separate documents or combined.

title: TONU
summary: Real freight-terminal photographs show trailers and freight operations that can be affected by cancellations. They do not prove that a TONU occurred or establish a fee.

items.label: TRAILERS AT A LOADING-DOCK WAREHOUSE
items.alt: 1980 photograph of trailer trucks parked at a loading-dock warehouse in Franklin County, Ohio.
items.caption: A trailer-terminal context; no cancellation or charge is shown.
items.credit: David E. Lucas / Columbus Metropolitan Library · No Copyright — United States

items.label: EMPTY FLATBED TRAILER
items.alt: Side view of an empty four-axle flatbed semitrailer.
items.caption: The source identifies an empty flatbed; emptiness alone does not establish a TONU or dispatch status.

facts.what: TONU means “truck ordered, not used” in common freight billing usage: a carrier may seek compensation when a load is cancelled after a truck has been ordered or dispatched.
facts.does: Eligibility, timing, required notice, and amount depend on the rate confirmation, customer terms, and facts of the cancellation.
facts.where: Record the load reference, dispatch status, notice time, and agreed contract terms.

note: There is no universal TONU amount. These photographs do not show a cancellation or claim.

sources.title: Context only — FMCSA — Broker and carrier arrangements are governed by applicable agreements and regulations

details.heading: Record the event
details.text: Document the accepted load, dispatch, cancellation time, truck position, communications, and agreed charge. Whether compensation is owed depends on the rate confirmation and other contract terms.

details.heading: Related charges
details.text: TONU addresses a load that does not move after a truck is ordered or committed. Detention addresses qualifying waiting time; a contract determines whether either charge applies.

title: FSC
summary: A real fuel-tanker photograph and a truck aftertreatment-system photograph provide fuel-operation context; no rate formula or pump price is shown.

items.label: FUEL DELIVERY TANKER
items.alt: Photograph of a fuel tanker tractor-trailer at a California service station.
items.caption: The source identifies a fuel-delivery tanker, a bulk fuel transport example.

items.label: FREIGHT CARRIER TRACTOR
items.alt: Photograph of a Freightliner tractor parked at a California travel plaza.
items.caption: This vehicle photo does not identify the carrier’s fuel cost or applied surcharge.

facts.what: A fuel surcharge (FSC) is a rate adjustment intended to address fuel-price changes. The calculation and index, baseline, schedule, and payer depend on the contract.
facts.does: An FSC may be a cents-per-mile table or a formula tied to a published index; do not assume one method is universal.
facts.where: Check the signed rate confirmation or contract for the selected index, base price, calculation, and applicable miles.

note: A fuel surcharge is contractual. The photos show fuel transport and a truck; they do not display a surcharge or diesel price.

sources.title: U.S. Energy Information Administration — Weekly retail diesel prices
FMCSA — Motor carrier registration and broker/carrier resources

details.heading: A contract-driven adjustment
details.text: An FSC formula may use a published fuel index, a baseline price, a fuel-economy assumption, and an agreed mileage basis. The contract defines timing, rounding, exclusions, and the party charged.

details.heading: Simple illustration
details.text: If an agreement sets a surcharge of $0.20 per loaded mile and the billable distance is 1,000 loaded miles, the surcharge is $200. This is an example, not a universal rate or formula.

title: Detention Calculation
summary: Freight-terminal photographs show trucks and cargo operations where waiting can occur. They do not show appointment times or prove chargeable detention.

items.label: FREIGHT-HOUSE LOADING ACTIVITY
items.alt: 1942 photograph of truck trailers at a Chicago freight house loading and unloading goods.
items.caption: A historical freight-house scene; wait time and contract terms are not visible.
items.credit: Jack Delano / U.S. Office of War Information · U.S. federal government work

items.alt: 1980 photograph of trailer trucks parked at a loading-dock warehouse in Franklin County, Ohio.
items.caption: A terminal context; parked trailers do not establish a detention event.

facts.what: Detention is compensation for qualifying time a truck is held beyond contractually allowed free time at pickup or delivery.
facts.does: A basic example is chargeable hours × the agreed hourly rate, often with rounding, caps, or separate terms. Start/end timestamps and free-time definitions matter.
facts.where: Keep arrival, check-in, dock, release, and departure timestamps with the load records.

note: No universal free-time allowance or hourly rate applies. Verify the rate confirmation and facility rules.

sources.title: FMCSA — Impact of driver detention time on safety and operations

details.heading: Worked example
details.text: If the contract allows two hours free and recognizes a documented four-hour wait, two hours may be chargeable. At an agreed $75 per hour, the example is 2 × $75 = $150 before any contractual rounding, caps, or exclusions.

details.heading: Evidence and terms
details.text: Record the times and events specified in the agreement, such as arrival, check-in, release, and departure. Appointment compliance, notice deadlines, approvals, and the party responsible can change the amount or eligibility.

title: Invoice Packet

items.alt: Photograph captioned by its author as a less-than-loaded truck ready for unloading.
items.caption: A freight movement example; it does not establish proof of delivery or billing status.

facts.what: A carrier invoice packet commonly includes an invoice, rate confirmation or load tender, bill of lading, proof of delivery, and approved accessorial evidence as required by the customer.
facts.does: Match every document to the same load reference; confirm the rate, delivered quantity, signatures or electronic evidence, and accessorial approvals before submission.
facts.where: Submit through the customer’s stated billing channel and keep a copy of the complete packet.

note: Packet contents and billing deadlines are customer- and contract-specific. The photos show freight activity only, not documents.

sources.title: Context only — FMCSA — Records and regulatory resources

details.heading: Build from the agreement
details.text: Match the invoice to the customer’s purchase order, load or reference number, rate, agreed accessorials, and required delivery evidence. Packet requirements vary by customer and contract.

details.heading: Avoid delays
details.text: Check that signatures or electronic delivery evidence are legible, dates match the shipment, and supporting approvals and timestamps accompany accessorial charges. Keep the original records according to applicable requirements.

title: Net 30
summary: Freight photographs provide shipment context for receivables. They do not display payment terms or a due date.

items.label: TRAILERS AT A FREIGHT CUSTOMER SITE
items.alt: 1980 photograph of trailer trucks at a loading-dock warehouse in Ohio.
items.caption: A freight customer context image; no invoice or payment term is visible.
items.credit: David E. Lucas / Columbus Metropolitan Library · No Copyright — United States

items.label: FREIGHT OPERATIONS
items.alt: 1942 photograph of truck trailers at a freight house.
items.caption: The photograph predates current payment systems and is used only as transport context.
items.credit: Jack Delano / U.S. Office of War Information · U.S. federal government work

facts.what: Net 30 usually means payment is due 30 calendar days from the date defined by the contract, such as invoice date or receipt of an approved invoice.
facts.does: The triggering date, business-day treatment, disputes, and late fees are controlled by the agreement and applicable law.
facts.where: Read the invoice terms and customer contract; calculate the due date from the stated trigger, not an assumed universal convention.

note: Net 30 is a payment term, not a guaranteed payment date. The photographs do not depict billing terms.

sources.title: Context only — U.S. Small Business Administration — Manage your finances

details.heading: Find the start date
details.text: Count from the date defined in the agreement. Invoice date, receipt date, and acceptance of a complete invoice packet can produce different due dates.

details.heading: Example
details.text: If a contract specifies 30 calendar days from an invoice dated June 1, the due date is July 1. Confirm any terms for weekends, disputes, or payment processing.

title: Freight Factoring
summary: Freight photographs show the underlying delivery operations. Factoring is a separate financial transaction involving receivables and a factor.

items.label: LTL FREIGHT MOVEMENT
items.alt: Photograph captioned by its author as a less-than-loaded truck ready for unloading.
items.caption: A real carrier-service context; no invoice sale is shown.

items.label: TRUCK FREIGHT LOADING
items.alt: 1965 U.S. Army photograph of cargo cartons being loaded onto a truck at Cam Ranh Bay.
items.caption: A loading context; it does not show a commercial factoring arrangement.

facts.what: Freight factoring is a transaction in which a carrier sells or assigns eligible invoices/receivables to a factor for earlier cash, generally for a fee and subject to contract terms.
facts.does: Advance rate, fees, recourse, reserves, notification, and eligibility vary. Compare the full agreement and customer/payment effects.
facts.where: Review an actual factoring agreement and invoice terms; do not infer the cost from a quoted advance alone.

note: This is a general business description, not individual financial advice. The photos are transport context, not evidence of a factoring service. Terms and legal effects must be checked against the factor agreement; no primary contract example is included.

details.heading: How cash moves
details.text: A factor advances part of an eligible receivable, collects according to the agreement, then settles any reserve less fees and adjustments. The advance is not the same as the total net proceeds.

details.heading: Compare contracts
details.text: Review recourse and non-recourse terms, reserve release, minimums, fees, notice of assignment, customer credit limits, and handling of disputed invoices. A factor’s collection rights depend on the contract and applicable law.

title: Downtime
summary: Real truck components and an inspection-site photo show maintenance and availability contexts; no duration or cause is inferred.

items.label: TRUCK AT INSPECTION SITE
items.alt: Oregon Department of Transportation photograph of a truck at an inspection station.
items.caption: The photo does not establish a breakdown or time out of service.
items.credit: Oregon Department of Transportation · CC BY 2.0

items.label: TRUCK AIR COMPRESSOR
items.alt: Photograph of a truck air compressor with Cummins branding.
items.caption: A component that can appear in a maintenance workflow; this photo does not show a failed compressor.

facts.what: Downtime is time equipment is unavailable for its planned work because of maintenance, repair, inspection, waiting, or another operational constraint.
facts.does: Track start/end definitions consistently and separate planned from unplanned downtime when managing availability.
facts.where: Record the unit, reason, start and return-to-service times, and resulting missed or reassigned work.

note: Downtime definitions differ by fleet. The images do not show a confirmed failure or elapsed downtime.

sources.title: Context only — FMCSA — Inspection, repair, and maintenance

details.heading: Define the clock
details.text: Specify whether downtime begins at breakdown, arrival in the shop, or missed dispatch, and whether it ends at repair completion or return to service. Consistent definitions make fleet comparisons useful.

details.heading: Diagnose the cost
details.text: Break out repair labor and parts, towing, replacement equipment, lost productive time, and other contract-specific costs. Avoid double-counting a missed load and a replacement expense.

title: Deadhead
summary: Photographs show a real empty flatbed and a freight truck. Empty miles are a dispatch/accounting condition and must be verified from the trip.

items.label: EMPTY FLATBED SEMITRAILER
items.alt: Side view of an empty four-axle flatbed semitrailer.
items.caption: The source describes this trailer as empty; the image alone does not show whether it is moving without a load or being repositioned.

items.label: LTL TRUCK READY TO UNLOAD
items.alt: Photograph captioned by its author as a less-than-loaded truck ready for unloading.
items.caption: This is a partially loaded/less-than-loaded freight context, not a deadhead proof.

facts.what: Deadhead miles are vehicle miles driven without revenue freight, often to reach a pickup or reposition after delivery.
facts.does: An empty deck does not always mean deadhead: the tractor may be under a paid movement, bobtailing, or repositioning under a contract. Define the metric consistently.
facts.where: Use dispatch/load records and odometer or telematics miles to classify loaded and empty miles.

note: The photographs do not verify trip status or revenue treatment. Deadhead definitions vary by carrier and contract.

sources.title: Context only — FMCSA — Motor carrier operations and records

details.heading: Measure consistently
details.text: Record miles driven without revenue freight and choose a consistent denominator for a deadhead percentage, such as total miles. A 100-mile empty repositioning trip on a 500-mile total trip is 20% of total miles.

details.heading: Operational tradeoff
details.text: A repositioning move can still be economically useful if it enables a better next load. Compare total trip revenue, cost, time, and available alternatives rather than judging one percentage in isolation.

title: Power Swap
summary: Photographs show tractors and trailers as separate equipment types. They do not document a particular tractor exchange.

items.label: TRACTOR WITH TRAILER

items.caption: A tractor–trailer combination illustrates that tractor power unit and trailer are separable equipment.

items.label: TRACTOR EXAMPLE

items.caption: A separate tractor example; it is not evidence that a power-only swap occurred.

facts.what: A power swap commonly describes changing the tractor/power unit while leaving a trailer in place or transferring it to another tractor, but carrier terminology can vary.
facts.does: Confirm which party supplies tractor, driver, trailer, insurance, and responsibility for securement, documents, and equipment condition.
facts.where: At the tractor–trailer coupling point, under an agreed dispatch and interchange process.

note: The term is not a single universal regulatory definition. These photos show tractors and a tractor–trailer, not a swap event or interchange record.

sources.title: Context only — FMCSA — Intermodal equipment and motor-carrier regulations

details.heading: Define the arrangement
details.text: A power-unit change can keep a trailer moving when a tractor or driver changes, but carrier terminology differs. Document the unit and trailer identifiers, condition, location, custody, and dispatch instructions at the exchange.
